title: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
summary: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound, how fusion cuts HBM bytes and launches, vertical vs horizontal and epilogue fusion, FlashAttention, the limits, and how TorchInductor and XLA decide.
outcomes: Explain why elementwise ops are memory bound using arithmetic intensity and the roofline ridge
Compute bytes moved and a bandwidth-bound speedup for an op chain before and after fusion
Distinguish vertical, horizontal and epilogue fusion and give a real example of each
Explain the limits of fusion: on-chip capacity, reductions, recomputation and saved activations
Describe how TorchInductor scores and applies fusions and how XLA defines a fusion

lessons.title: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound

blocks.md:
A transformer MLP block often ends in a chain like this: scale each element by a per-channel weight, add a bias, apply GELU, apply dropout. Each step is **elementwise** (also called pointwise): output element i depends only on input element i.

In PyTorch eager mode, every one of those ops is a separate GPU **kernel** (a function launched on the GPU). A kernel reads its inputs from **HBM** (the GPU's off-chip high bandwidth memory), computes, and writes its output back to HBM. The next kernel starts by reading that output again.

Our running example: `x` has shape 8192 x 4096 in BF16 (2 bytes per element), so $N = 33{,}554{,}432$ elements and 64 MiB per full tensor. The weight `w` and bias `b` are per-channel vectors of 4096 elements (8 KiB each), small enough to ignore in most of the arithmetic.

We run it on a model GPU with the A100 80GB datasheet numbers: 2,039 GB/s of HBM bandwidth and 19.5 TFLOPS of non-tensor-core FP32 math.

blocks.title: Eager mode: every op is a round trip through HBM

nodes.label:
one fused kernel
scale, shift, GELU, dropout

scenes.caption: Kernel 1 loads all of x (64 MiB of BF16) from HBM, multiplies each element by its channel weight, and writes the full result t1 back to HBM.
Kernel 2 reads t1 straight back from HBM just to add the bias, then writes t2. The data made a full trip off chip and back for one addition per element.
Kernel 3 reads t2, applies GELU, writes t3. Each kernel starts from HBM because kernels cannot hand registers or shared memory to the next kernel.
Kernel 4 reads t3 and writes the output y plus a 1-byte-per-element keep mask for the backward pass. Four launches, four full reads, four full writes plus a half-size mask write.
Fused: one kernel reads x once, keeps every intermediate in registers, and writes only y and the mask. t1, t2 and t3 never exist in HBM.

blocks.md:
From the roofline course: a kernel's **arithmetic intensity** is FLOPs per byte moved, and a kernel whose intensity is below the GPU's ridge point (peak FLOP/s divided by peak bytes/s) is limited by memory bandwidth, not math.

NVIDIA's performance guide lists ReLU at 0.25 FLOP/B and says elementwise layers tend to be memory limited because they do few operations per byte. FlashAttention's background section makes the same split: activation, dropout, softmax and layer norm are memory bound; big matmuls are compute bound.

blocks.title: Arithmetic intensity of each kernel vs the A100 FP32 ridge

scenes.caption: Simplified FLOP counts: GELU is 9 ops with tanh as one, dropout 3 ops per 5 bytes, random number generation ignored. The mul and add kernels do 1 FLOP per 4 bytes moved: 0.25 FLOP/B, the same figure NVIDIA lists for ReLU.
The ridge is 19.5 TFLOPS FP32 / 2,039 GB/s = 9.56 FLOP/B. Every eager kernel sits far left of it, so each one runs at memory speed and the ALUs mostly wait.
Fusing does about 14 FLOPs per 5 bytes: 2.8 FLOP/B. Still memory bound, but the bytes are now the minimum possible, so the kernel is as fast as this chain can be.

blocks.prompt: The GELU kernel does 9 times more math per element than the add kernel. If you replaced the add kernel's body with GELU's, roughly how much slower would that kernel get?
blocks.reveal:
**Almost not at all.** Both kernels move the same 4 bytes per element (read 2, write 2). At 2.25 FLOP/B GELU is still four times below the 9.56 ridge, so the extra math hides under the memory traffic. Time is set by bytes: 134 MB / 2,039 GB/s = 66 us either way.

This is the key insight behind fusion: in a memory-bound kernel, extra arithmetic is nearly free and extra bytes are what cost time.

blocks.md: For memory-bound kernels, runtime is roughly bytes moved / bandwidth. Elementwise ops do so little math per byte that the only lever that matters is how many bytes cross the HBM boundary. Fusion cuts bytes, not FLOPs.
Misconception: "the GPU is slow at GELU because tanh is expensive". Profile first. A standalone GELU kernel on a large tensor is limited by the read and the write of the tensor, not by tanh.

blocks.question: A colleague profiles the eager chain and sees the GPU's math units are about 5 percent busy during the four elementwise kernels. What does that most likely mean?
options: The kernels are badly written and should use tensor cores
The kernels are bandwidth bound: they spend their time waiting on HBM, which is expected at intensities far below the ridge
The GPU is thermally throttling
The tensor is too small to fill the GPU
blocks.explain: At 0.25 to 2.25 FLOP/B versus a 9.56 ridge, the math units must idle most of the time while memory streams. Tensor cores do not help elementwise ops; the fix is moving fewer bytes, which is what fusion does.

blocks.question: Which of these operations is most likely compute bound on a modern GPU?
options: Adding a bias to a 64 MiB activation
Dropout on a 64 MiB activation
An 8192 x 4096 by 4096 x 4096 matrix multiply
Layer norm over 4096 channels
blocks.explain: The matmul does 2MNK = 275 GFLOP over about 168 MB of minimum traffic, around 1,600 FLOP/B, far above even the BF16 tensor-core ridge of about 153 FLOP/B. The other three are elementwise or reductions with intensity well under 10.

lessons.title: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion

blocks.md: Now count exactly. Write $N$ for the number of elements and assume BF16 (2 bytes). Each of mul, add and GELU reads one full tensor and writes one: $4N$ bytes each. Dropout reads one tensor, writes the output ($2N$) and writes a boolean keep mask ($N$, 1 byte per element) that backward will need.

blocks.title: HBM traffic per kernel (MB), eager vs fused

scenes.caption: Eager: mul, add and GELU each read one 67.1 MB tensor and write one (plus 8 KiB for w or b): 134.2 MB each.
Dropout reads t3 (67.1 MB), writes y (67.1 MB) and writes a 1-byte keep mask (33.6 MB): 167.8 MB. Eager total: 570.4 MB, or 17 bytes per element.
Fused: read x once (67.1 MB), write y (67.1 MB) and the mask (33.6 MB). 167.8 MB total, 5 bytes per element. The three 64 MiB temporaries vanish.

blocks.caption: Ignoring the two 8 KiB vectors w and b. With N = 33,554,432 this is 570.4 MB vs 167.8 MB.
Speedup bound = 17N / 5N = 3.4x. Real kernels reach less than peak bandwidth, but the ratio is what fusion buys.

blocks.prompt: The chain has four ops. Will fusing it give a 4x speedup?
blocks.reveal:
**About 3.4x in the bandwidth model, not 4x.** Fusion removes the intermediate traffic but not the unavoidable traffic: you must still read x and write y, and the mask write (1 byte per element) is extra output that does not shrink. 17 / 5 = 3.4.

The general rule: speedup = (bytes eager) / (bytes fused), and the fused number is set by the inputs you must read and the outputs you must keep.

scenes.caption: Eager, if each kernel streams at full bandwidth: 65.8 + 65.8 + 65.8 + 82.3 = 279.8 us. Launch gaps between kernels are ignored here (simplified).
Fused: 167.8 MB / 2,039 GB/s = 82.3 us, the same time eager spends on the dropout kernel alone. Speedup 279.8 / 82.3 = 3.40x.

blocks.md: Bytes are not the only cost. Each kernel launch has a fixed CPU and GPU overhead, and on a small tensor the four launches can take longer than the data movement itself. Fusion removes launches too, which is why it helps even tiny tensors. The exact launch cost depends on the system, so the next figure treats it as a slider rather than a fact. (Separately, CUDA Graphs attack launch overhead without fusing; TorchInductor uses them when static analysis shows it is safe and they are enabled.)

blocks.title: Eager vs fused time as tensor size grows (model)

scenes.caption: With no launch cost, both lines are pure bandwidth: the fused line is always 17/5 = 3.4x lower. The points mark our 33.5M element example.
Add an assumed 5 us per launch. On small tensors the curves flatten at 20 us vs 5 us: launches dominate and fusion saves launches, approaching a 4x ratio.
Raise bandwidth to 8 TB/s. Bytes get cheaper, so fixed launch costs matter up to larger sizes. Fusion helps in both regimes, for different reasons.

blocks.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def chain(x, w, b):
    h = F.gelu(x * w + b, approximate="tanh")
    return F.dropout(h, p=0.1, training=True)

x = torch.randn(8192, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
w = torch.randn(4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
b = torch.randn(4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

y = chain(x, w, b)                # eager: one kernel per op
fast = torch.compile(chain)       # TorchInductor emits Triton for the GPU
y2 = fast(x, w, b)
# See fusion decisions and kernels: TORCH_LOGS=fusion,output_code python script.py
blocks.caption: The same chain in eager mode and under torch.compile. Dropout uses random numbers, so y and y2 will not be bitwise equal.

blocks.md: Fused bytes = what you must read + what you must keep. Everything in between is the saving. For a chain of k unary elementwise ops on the same tensor with no side outputs, eager moves about k times the fused bytes.

blocks.question: Same chain, but at inference (dropout disabled, so no mask and no dropout kernel). What is the bandwidth-model speedup from fusing scale, shift and GELU?
options: 3x
4x
blocks.explain: Eager: three kernels at 4N bytes each = 12N. Fused: read x (2N) and write the output (2N) = 4N. 12N / 4N = 3x.

blocks.question: You fuse the chain but your profiler shows the fused kernel at 140 us instead of the 82 us model. Which explanation fits best?
options: Fusion added too many FLOPs and made it compute bound
Fused kernels cannot use HBM
BF16 math is emulated in FP32 and is slow
The model assumed peak HBM bandwidth; real kernels reach less than peak, so compare against eager measured the same way
blocks.explain: At 2.8 FLOP/B the fused kernel is still far below the 9.56 ridge, so it is not compute bound. The model is an upper bound on speed: achieved bandwidth is below the datasheet peak. Compare against eager measured the same way.

blocks.md:
Lesson 2 fused a straight chain where each op consumes the previous op's output. That is **vertical fusion** (producer-consumer fusion). The intermediate value lives in a register between ops instead of in HBM.

A second kind exists. **Horizontal fusion** merges ops that do *not* depend on each other but run over the same data or the same shape: siblings. The PyTorch 2 paper calls these consumer/consumer fusions, and TorchInductor's scheduler does both kinds.

scenes.caption: A small graph. Top: a producer-consumer chain. Bottom: two independent reductions that both read x and do not depend on each other.
Vertical fusion merges a producer with its consumer: scale, shift and GELU become one kernel, and the values pass between them in registers.
Horizontal fusion merges siblings that share an input: one kernel reads x once and computes both sums. Saves one full read of x and one launch.

blocks.md:
Horizontal fusion's savings come from two places. If siblings read the same input, the shared read happens once: for our 64 MiB `x`, computing `sum(x)` and `sum(x * x)` in separate kernels reads 134.2 MB, while one kernel reads 67.1 MB (32.9 us instead of 65.8 us at 2,039 GB/s).

If siblings read different inputs, there are no shared bytes, but there are fewer launches. That case matters when there are many small tensors, which is exactly the shape of an optimizer step.

blocks.title: Two reductions over x: separate vs horizontally fused

scenes.caption: Separate kernels: each reduction streams the full 67.1 MB tensor. 134.2 MB total.
Fused: one pass loads each element once and updates both accumulators. 67.1 MB total, half the traffic. The outputs are tiny, so writes do not matter here.

blocks.md:
**Optimizers are the classic case.** An Adam step applies the same handful of elementwise updates to every parameter tensor, often hundreds of separate tensors. A plain for-loop launches several kernels per tensor.

- `foreach=True` (PyTorch's default on CUDA when you set neither flag) uses multi-tensor kernels that process a list of tensors per launch: horizontal fusion across parameters.
- `fused=True` also merges the elementwise update math into one kernel. PyTorch's docs describe it as theoretically fastest, with both vertical and horizontal fusion.
- NVIDIA Apex's `FusedAdam` describes the same two fusions: the update's elementwise ops, and a multi-tensor apply launch that batches all parameters into one or a few launches.

blocks.code:
import torch
model = torch.nn.Linear(4096, 4096).cuda()

# for-loop: several kernels per parameter tensor
opt_loop = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, foreach=False)
# foreach: multi-tensor kernels, horizontal fusion across params
opt_each = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, foreach=True)
# fused: one kernel does the whole update (vertical + horizontal)
opt_fuse = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, fused=True)
blocks.caption: The three Adam implementations in torch.optim. The math is the same; the number of launches and HBM passes differs.

blocks.prompt: The foreach Adam is usually faster than the for-loop version. Is there any cost?
blocks.reveal: **Yes: memory.** PyTorch's docs note that the foreach implementation uses about sizeof(params) more peak memory than the for-loop, because its intermediates are whole lists of tensors rather than one tensor at a time. Horizontal fusion often trades peak memory for fewer launches.

blocks.md: Quick test for which kind you are looking at: if op B reads op A's output, fusing them is vertical. If A and B are independent but iterate over the same data or the same index space, fusing them is horizontal.

blocks.question: Which pair is a horizontal fusion opportunity?
options: GELU applied to the output of a bias add
Updating 300 parameter tensors with the same Adam formula in one launch
A softmax whose output feeds a matmul
A dropout applied after GELU
blocks.explain: The 300 parameter updates are independent of one another and run the same code, so batching them into one launch is horizontal. The other three are producer-consumer pairs, which is vertical fusion.

blocks.question: Two sibling kernels each read a different 1 KB tensor. What does horizontal fusion mainly save?
options: Half of the HBM traffic
Nothing; fusion only helps when inputs are shared
One kernel launch's fixed overhead
Register pressure
blocks.explain: No bytes are shared, so traffic is unchanged. With tiny tensors the runtime is dominated by fixed launch cost, and merging two launches into one removes one of those costs.

lessons.title: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention

blocks.md:
Elementwise chains are easy to fuse with each other. The harder and very common case is an elementwise op right after a **matmul**, such as a linear layer followed by bias and GELU. The matmul is a library call (cuBLAS) or a carefully tiled template, not a simple loop a compiler can merge into.

The answer is **epilogue fusion**. CUTLASS's GEMM design describes the **epilogue** as a separate phase after the main loop, where results held in registers are written out and where linear scaling and other elementwise operations can conveniently be applied.

blocks.title: Epilogue fusion: finish the math before the tile leaves the chip

scenes.caption: A GEMM kernel streams tiles of A and B through tensor cores and accumulates one output tile in registers. This is the compute-bound part.
Unfused: the tile is stored to HBM as plain D, then a second kernel reads all of D back, adds bias, applies GELU and writes it again: 134.2 MB of extra traffic.
Fused epilogue: bias and GELU are applied to the accumulator tile while it is still in registers, then stored once. The separate kernel and its round trip disappear.

blocks.md:
Vendor libraries expose this too. cuBLASLt takes an epilogue setting: `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_BIAS`, `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_RELU_BIAS`, `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_BIAS`, and `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_AUX_BIAS`, which also outputs the GELU input as a separate matrix, described as useful for training. Backward variants such as `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_DGELU_BGRAD` apply the GELU gradient and compute the bias gradient in the same call.

TorchInductor can generate matmuls from its own Triton templates with pointwise epilogue fusion instead of calling cuBLAS; its autotuner (`mode="max-autotune"`) chooses when to use them.

scenes.caption: 2MNK = 274.9 GFLOP at 312 TFLOPS BF16 = 881.0 us. Its 167.8 MB of minimum traffic would take only 82.3 us, so math dominates.
A separate bias + GELU kernel moves 134.2 MB: 65.8 us more, 947 us total. About 7 percent of the layer is pure round trip.
Epilogue fused: the extra kernel is gone. For training, a GELU_AUX style epilogue also writes the GELU input for backward: one extra 67.1 MB write, 32.9 us, still half the unfused cost.

blocks.md: Epilogue fusion matters less than elementwise fusion for big GEMMs: the matmul is compute bound and dominates, so removing a 66 us kernel from a 947 us layer saves about 7 percent. It matters more for small or skinny matmuls, where the GEMM itself is short.

**Reductions can be fused too, if the data fits on chip.** Triton's fused softmax tutorial counts that a naive PyTorch softmax over an M x N matrix reads $5MN + 2M$ elements and writes $3MN + 2M$, because max, subtract, exp, sum and divide are separate kernels. A fused kernel loads each row once into SRAM, does all five steps on chip and writes once: $MN$ reads and $MN$ writes, a theoretical speedup of about 4x. The catch, in the tutorial's own framing: it works for matrices whose rows fit in the GPU's SRAM.

**FlashAttention is fusion of the whole attention block.** Standard attention computes $S = QK^T$, writes it to HBM, reads it for softmax, writes $P$, reads $P$ for $PV$. FlashAttention computes matmul, softmax, optional masking and dropout, and the second matmul in one CUDA kernel. Rows of $S$ are far too long to fit in SRAM, so it adds tiling with a running (online) softmax, and recomputes attention blocks in the backward pass instead of storing the $N \times N$ matrix. Its paper proves standard attention needs $\Theta(Nd + N^2)$ HBM accesses versus $\Theta(N^2 d^2 M^{-1})$ for FlashAttention, where $M$ is SRAM size.

blocks.prompt: Why could a generic elementwise fuser not have produced FlashAttention on its own?
blocks.reveal: Attention contains **two matmuls and a row reduction (softmax) whose rows are longer than SRAM**. Merging ops into one kernel is not enough when an intermediate (a full row of S) does not fit on chip. FlashAttention needed an algorithm change: tile over keys, keep a running max and sum, rescale partial outputs, and recompute in backward. Fusion opportunities are limited by what fits on chip, not just by the graph.

blocks.question: A training step uses `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_AUX_BIAS` instead of `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_BIAS`. Why?
options: AUX makes the forward GELU more accurate
AUX disables the bias for the backward pass
AUX is required for BF16 outputs
Backward needs the GELU input, and AUX writes it out in the same kernel instead of a separate pass
blocks.explain: GELU's derivative depends on its input. Without saving the pre-activation, backward would have to recompute it from the matmul. The AUX epilogue writes it as a side output while the tile is already on chip.

blocks.question: Using the Triton tutorial's count, what is the softmax speedup bound for M = N = 4096?
options: About 2x
About 3x
About 4x
About 8x
blocks.explain: Naive: (5MN + 2M) + (3MN + 2M) = 8MN + 4M element accesses. Fused: 2MN. Ratio (8MN + 4M) / 2MN = 4.0005 for M = N = 4096.

lessons.title: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide

blocks.md:
If fusion is so good, why not fuse a whole model into one kernel? Because a kernel has hard limits:

- **On-chip capacity and register pressure.** Every value kept live across fused ops occupies registers or shared memory. Too many live values means fewer threads resident per SM (lower occupancy) or spills to slower memory. Triton's softmax tutorial targets rows that fit in SRAM for exactly this reason.
- **Reductions and different shapes.** A reduction changes the iteration space; its consumers need the finished result. Fusing reduction, broadcast and another reduction (layer norm's pattern) needs backend support; the PyTorch 2 paper notes Inductor supports it for Triton but not C++.
- **Access order.** If a producer writes in forward order but the consumer reads in reverse, the paper's example, the two cannot be fused.

- **Library boundaries.** XLA's GPU docs note that vendor libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN are fast and verified but often preclude complex fusion; that is why epilogues and Triton templates exist.
- **Recomputation.** Merging a producer into several consumers duplicates its work in each one. TorchInductor's inlining does this deliberately for cheap pointwise bodies when thresholds are met.
- **Training needs saved activations.** The FlashAttention paper points out that intermediates still have to be written to HBM for the backward pass, which reduces the benefit of naive fusion.

blocks.title: Training the chain: save the GELU input or recompute it?

scenes.caption: Backward needs GELU's input t2. Eager already wrote t2 to HBM, so it costs no extra traffic there: 570.4 MB.
A fused kernel never stores t2. Writing it as a side output adds 67.1 MB: 234.9 MB, speedup over eager falls from 3.40x to 2.43x.
Since x is saved anyway (the weight gradient needs it), backward can recompute t2 = x times w plus b for 2 FLOPs per element. Forward stays at 167.8 MB.

blocks.md: PyTorch automates that last choice. AOTAutograd traces a joint forward and backward graph and splits it with a min-cut algorithm that optimizes memory, and as part of it rematerializes activations that are cheap to recompute in backward. FlashAttention makes the same trade by hand: store the output and softmax statistics, recompute attention blocks in backward.

**How TorchInductor decides.** After lowering, the scheduler wraps each buffer in a node and derives dependency edges from memory reads and writes. Two functions drive fusion: `can_fuse(a, b)` (legality plus heuristics; the paper's example is that with `config.aggressive_fusion=False` it refuses nodes that share no memory accesses, which current source enforces with a minimum shared-bytes threshold) and `score_fusion(a, b)` (ranks by category, estimated bytes saved, then graph distance). A greedy loop applies the best legal fusions until none remain.

blocks.title: TorchInductor's greedy fusion loop (simplified)

scenes.caption: Start with one scheduler node per buffer. Simplified: Inductor usually inlines pointwise ops during lowering, so a real graph arrives partly fused.
can_fuse checks dependency edges and legality. sum_x shares a read of x with scale, so it is a horizontal candidate.
score_fusion orders by fusion category, then estimated bytes of memory traffic saved, then shorter distance in the original graph. Producer-consumer pairs save a whole 64 MiB write and read.
Apply each candidate that is still legal. Pending candidates that pointed at merged nodes are rewired to the new fused node.
Fusions can open new opportunities, so the loop runs again until a round finds nothing. Here the pointwise group and sum_x may merge horizontally.
Next round: no candidates remain, so the loop exits. Each remaining node becomes one generated Triton kernel.

blocks.md: **XLA** takes the same view and calls fusion its single most important optimization. Its GPU docs state two invariants: a fusion always compiles to exactly one GPU kernel, and no intermediate inside a fusion is materialized in HBM. For more advanced fusions that include a matmul or softmax, XLA:GPU generates code through Triton.

blocks.title: PyTorch 2 ablation: geomean speedup over eager (A100, HF fp16)

scenes.caption: Inference. Turning off fusion drops 1.91x to 1.68x; turning off inlining drops it to 1.58x. The passes overlap heavily, so either one alone recovers most of the benefit.
Training: 1.45x, 1.27x, 1.31x. Without both passes, compiled code is slower than eager (0.80x and 0.59x) because decompositions split big ops into small primitives that only fusion recombines.

blocks.md: A fusion is worth it when it removes HBM round trips or launches without blowing the on-chip budget or recomputing expensive work. Compilers estimate bytes saved, check legality, and fuse greedily; in training they also choose between saving and recomputing activations.

blocks.question: A compiler fuses an expensive producer (many FLOPs per element) into 6 different consumers by inlining it into each. What is the risk?
options: None, fusion never adds work
It always breaks numerical correctness
The producer's math now runs 6 times, which can turn a memory-bound saving into a compute cost
It forces the output into FP32
blocks.explain: Inlining duplicates the producer body into every consumer. For cheap pointwise ops the duplicated math is free under the memory bound; for expensive ones it can cost more than the HBM round trip it saved. Inductor inlines only when thresholds are met.

blocks.question: In the PyTorch 2 ablation, disabling both fusion and inlining made compiled models slower than eager. Why?
options: torch.compile adds Python overhead per op
Inductor decomposes large operators into many primitives and relies on fusion to recombine them
Triton kernels are slower than CUDA kernels
Graph breaks increase without fusion
blocks.explain: The paper explains that decompositions break large optimized operators into smaller primitive ops, and fusion recombines them. Without fusion and inlining each primitive becomes its own kernel with its own HBM round trip, so the result is slower than eager's hand-written kernels.

blocks.question: A fused kernel for a long row-wise reduction starts spilling registers and runs slower than two unfused kernels. Which fix matches what FlashAttention and Triton tutorials do?
options: Tile the reduction so each block of the row fits on chip, carrying running statistics between tiles
Fuse even more ops into the kernel
Switch to FP64 to get more registers
Disable the GPU's L2 cache
blocks.explain: Fusion is bounded by on-chip capacity. Tiling with running statistics (as in FlashAttention's online softmax) keeps the working set small while still avoiding HBM round trips for intermediates.
